questions.question: Recognize the importance of preservation in maintaining food safety. a). It helps delay spoilage and maintain food in a safer and acceptable condition b). It increases the risk of food deterioration c). It eliminates the need for hygienic food handling d). It reduces the storage life of food
questions.solution_html:
• Flavour enhancement: Spices improve the taste and palatability of food. For example, black
  • pepper provides pungency, while cinnamon gives a warm, sweet flavour.
  • Harvesting: Mature nutmeg fruits are harvested when the outer fruit turns yellow and splits
  • open naturally, before the fruits deteriorate.
  • Spent spice (spent material): The solid residue remaining after solvent or supercritical CO₂
  • extraction. It may contain residual essential oils, fibre, carbohydrates and proteins.
  • Selection of raw material: Select fresh, mature, aromatic spices such as black pepper, cardamom
  • ginger, turmeric or clove with good flavour and quality.
  • Piperine: The major pungent alkaloid responsible for the characteristic sharp taste of black
  • pepper. It contributes to the spice’s commercial and functional value.
  • Vanillin formation: Enzymatic hydrolysis converts glucovanillin into vanillin, the principal
  • compound responsible for the characteristic flavour and aroma of vanilla.
  • Maximum essential oil content: Fully mature capsules contain well-developed seeds with a
  • high concentration of volatile oils responsible for the characteristic aroma and flavour.
  • Flower collection: Flowers are collected carefully, preferably during the cool morning hours
  • to minimise damage and preserve freshness.
  • V olatile fraction (essential oil fraction)
  • This fraction contains volatile aromatic compounds responsible mainly for the characteristic aroma
  • and flavour of spices.
  • • Monoterpenes: Examples include limonene, α-pinene, β-pinene and sabinene. They contribute
  • fresh, citrus-like and herbal aromas.
  • • Sesquiterpenes: Examples include caryophyllene, zingiberene and humulene. They contribute
  • warm, spicy, woody and earthy aromas.
  • • Oxygenated terpenoids: These include alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, phenols, esters and
  • oxides that contribute to aroma, flavour and biological activity.
  • Aroma: Provide the characteristic smell of the spice.
  • Pungency: Compounds such as piperine and capsaicin provide the characteristic pungent
  • sensation.
  • Coriander powder
  • Coriander powder is produced by cleaning, drying and grinding coriander seeds.
  • Steps involved
  • Harvesting: Coriander plants are harvested when the fruits reach physiological maturity.
  • Cleaning: Coriander seeds are cleaned to remove foreign matter.
  • Flavour enhancement
  • • Spices impart distinctive flavour characteristics and improve the palatability of food.
  • • Different spices provide sweet, warm, earthy, pungent or bitter flavour notes.
  • • Black pepper provides a sharp flavour due to piperine, while cinnamon provides a warm
  • sweet flavour due to cinnamaldehyde.
  • • Spice combinations produce distinctive flavours in regional and international cuisines.
  • Cinnamon
  • Active compound: Cinnamaldehyde.
  • Dietary uses
  • • Used in cakes, biscuits, chocolates, desserts and confectionery.
  • • Added to beverages, breakfast cereals and spice blends.
  • • Provides a warm, sweet aroma and characteristic flavour.
  • Medicinal significance
  • • Contains antioxidant compounds.
  • • Exhibits antimicrobial activity in laboratory studies.
  • • Has been studied for potential effects on blood glucose regulation.
  • • Traditionally used to support digestion.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Identify the compound associated with the characteristic warm spicy flavour of cumin. a). Linalool b). Cuminaldehyde c). Eugenol d). Anethole
questions.solution_html:
• Aroma development: V olatile compounds contribute to the characteristic aroma of foods.
  • Eugenol in clove and cinnamaldehyde in cinnamon are examples.
  • Splitting: The outer fruit is removed or allowed to split open to expose the nutmeg seed
  • surrounded by the reddish aril.
  • Spent herbal biomass: The remaining plant material after extraction of herbs or spices. It can be
  • used for composting, organic fertiliser production, bioenergy production and soil conditioning.
  • Cleaning: Remove foreign materials such as dust, stones, soil and plant debris to ensure the purity
  • of the final product.
  • V olatile oils: These provide the characteristic aroma and flavour. Important constituents
  • include pinene, limonene and caryophyllene.
  • Flavour development: Curing develops the characteristic sweet, pleasant and complex flavour
  • of vanilla. Sweating is particularly important for flavour development.
  • Better flavour and aroma: Harvesting at the appropriate maturity ensures the development of
  • the desirable cardamom flavour and aroma.
  • Stigma separation: The red stigmas are separated manually from the flowers without
  • damaging or mixing them with unwanted floral parts.
  • Non-volatile fraction (resinous fraction)
  • This fraction contains non-volatile compounds responsible for the body, colour, pungency and
  • persistence of flavour.
  • • Resins: High-molecular-weight compounds that provide viscosity, body and flavour retention.
  • • Natural pigments: Curcumin in turmeric, capsanthin and capsorubin in paprika, and
  • chlorophyll in herbs contribute characteristic colours.
  • • Pungent principles: Piperine in black pepper, capsaicin in chilli, and gingerol in fresh ginger
  • contribute characteristic pungency.
  • • Fixed oils: Non-volatile triglycerides present in certain spices, such as nutmeg, coriander and
  • black pepper, contribute to the composition and stability of oleoresins.
  • • Waxes: Present in small quantities, they protect plant tissues and increase the viscosity and
  • stability of oleoresins.
  • Role of volatile and non-volatile constituents
  • A. V olatile constituents
  • Flavour: Contribute to the overall sensory profile of the extract.
  • Colour: Natural pigments contribute the characteristic colour of the oleoresin.
  • Threshing: The dried or harvested plant material is threshed to separate the coriander fruits
  • from the stems.
  • Coriander oleoresin
  • Coriander oleoresin is a concentrated extract containing volatile and non-volatile constituents
  • responsible for the characteristic flavour and aroma of coriander.
  • Steps involved
  • Drying: The seeds are dried to a suitable moisture level.
  • Taste and pungency
  • • Spices stimulate different taste and oral sensory responses.
  • • Piperine in black pepper and capsaicinoids in chilli produce pungency.
  • • Ginger contributes a warm, spicy sensation due to gingerols and related compounds.
  • • Appropriate amounts of spices enhance the overall eating experience, whereas excessive
  • amounts may cause undesirable intensity.
  • Clove
  • Active compound: Eugenol.
  • Dietary uses
  • • Used in spice blends, bakery products, pickles and beverages.
  • • Added to meat preparations, sauces and confectionery.
  • • Provides a strong, warm and aromatic flavour.
  • Medicinal significance
  • • Exhibits antioxidant and antimicrobial activity.
  • • Traditionally used for digestive discomfort.
  • • Clove oil is used in dentistry for its local analgesic properties under appropriate professional
  • guidance.

questions.question: Recognize the major volatile oil constituent responsible for the characteristic aroma of clove a). Eugenol b). Gingerol c). Piperine d). Curcumin

  • red colour due to carotenoid pigments.
  • Aril removal: The mace aril is carefully separated from the nutmeg seed by hand.
  • Recovered solvents: Organic solvents such as hexane, ethanol and acetone are recovered during
  • evaporation or solvent-recovery operations. They can be purified and reused, reducing production
  • costs and environmental pollution.
  • Drying: Dry the spices to an optimum moisture level to improve extraction efficiency and prevent
  • microbial growth.
  • Fixed oils: Black pepper contains non-volatile lipids that contribute to its chemical
  • composition.
  • Colour development: The green beans gradually develop their characteristic brown colour
  • during curing.
  • Prevention of seed loss: Harvesting before the capsules split prevents seeds from falling out
  • thereby reducing losses.
  • Drying: The stigmas are dried carefully under controlled conditions to reduce moisture and
  • prevent microbial spoilage.
  • Freshness: Their retention helps maintain the desirable aroma and flavour.
  • Flavour persistence: Resinous constituents help retain flavour for a longer period.
  • Cleaning: Dust, stones, stalks and other foreign materials are removed.
  • Grinding: The seeds are ground to an appropriate particle size to facilitate extraction.
  • Aroma development
  • • V olatile compounds in spices contribute to the characteristic aroma of foods.
  • • Eugenol in clove provides a strong, warm aroma.
  • • Cinnamaldehyde gives cinnamon its characteristic fragrance.
  • • Linalool contributes to the pleasant citrus-like aroma of coriander.
  • • Aroma strongly influences appetite and consumer perception of food quality.

  • • Added to confectionery, bakery products and beverages.
  • • Used in spice mixtures and traditional digestive preparations.

  • • Traditionally used as a digestive and carminative agent.
  • • May help relieve mild flatulence and bloating.

questions.question: Select the correct sequence for essential-oil manufacture by steam distillation. a). Grinding → steam distillation → condensation → separation → filtration b). Condensation → grinding → fermentation → separation c). Extraction → fermentation → drying → condensation d). Grinding → solvent extraction → crystallization
questions.solution_html:
• Food preservation: Certain spices possess antimicrobial and antioxidant properties that help
  • delay microbial spoilage and oxidative deterioration.
  • Washing: The separated mace blades are washed in clean water to remove dirt and other
  • impurities.
  • Carbon dioxide (CO₂ ): In supercritical CO₂ extraction, carbon dioxide is recovered after
  • separation and recycled for repeated extraction cycles. This reduces operating costs and solvent
  • related waste.
  • Grinding: Grind the dried spices to an appropriate particle size. This increases the surface area and
  • improves the penetration of supercritical CO₂ .
  • Resinous substances: These contribute to the flavour and other characteristics of pepper
  • extracts and oleoresins.
  • Moisture reduction: Controlled drying reduces moisture content, helping prevent fungal
  • growth and spoilage.
  • Colour retention: Mature green capsules retain their attractive green colour after proper
  • curing, improving their appearance and quality.
  • Colour preservation: Careful drying and protection from excessive heat and light help
  • preserve crocin, the principal colouring compound.
  • Biological activity: Certain compounds possess antimicrobial and antioxidant properties.
  • B. Non-volatile constituents
  • Body and viscosity: Resins contribute to the concentrated, viscous nature of oleoresins.
  • Drying: The seeds are dried to a suitable moisture level to improve storage stability and
  • prevent mould growth.
  • Solvent extraction: A suitable food-grade solvent is passed through or mixed with the ground
  • seeds to extract the desirable compounds.
  • Colour improvement
  • • Natural pigments in spices improve the visual appearance of food.
  • • Curcumin in turmeric imparts a yellow colour.
  • • Capsanthin and capsorubin in chilli contribute red colour.
  • • Saffron imparts a golden-yellow colour due to crocin.
  • • Attractive colour increases visual appeal and can improve consumer acceptance.
  • Fenugreek
  • Active constituents: Sotolon, saponins, alkaloids and mucilage.
  • Dietary uses
  • • Used in curry powders, pickles and traditional dishes.
  • • Added to spice blends and selected functional food products.
  • • Provides a characteristic bitter taste and strong aroma.
  • Medicinal significance
  • • Contains dietary fibre and other bioactive constituents.
  • • Has been studied for potential effects on blood glucose regulation.
  • • Has also been investigated for its possible role in cholesterol management.
  • • Traditionally used to support digestion.

questions.question: Recognize the commercial spice obtained from cured and dried rhizomes. a). Nutmeg b). Turmeric c). Fennel d). Clove
questions.solution_html:
• Digestive benefits: Ginger, cumin and fennel are traditionally used to support digestion and
  • relieve digestive discomfort.
  • Blanching (optional): Mace may be blanched in hot water at approximately 80–90°C for 1–2
  • minutes to help retain its colour.
  • Hydrosol (aromatic water): In processes involving steam or hydro-distillation, the aqueous layer
  • obtained along with essential oil may contain dissolved aromatic compounds. Depending on its
  • composition and quality, it may be used in suitable applications.
  • Compression of CO₂ : Carbon dioxide is compressed using a high-pressure pump and heated above
  • its critical temperature of approximately 31.1°C and critical pressure of 7.38 MPa (73.8 bar).
  • Carbohydrates: Include starch and other carbohydrates that contribute to the bulk of the spice.
  • Texture improvement: Proper curing produces flexible beans without making them
  • excessively brittle.
  • Improved market value: Uniform, green and aromatic capsules receive better commercial
  • acceptance and higher market value.
  • Aroma preservation: Appropriate handling helps retain safranal and other volatile compounds
  • responsible for saffron’s characteristic aroma.
  • Stability: Resinous compounds improve flavour retention and contribute to greater chemical
  • stability during storage.
  • The volatile fraction primarily determines the aroma and contributes to flavour, whereas the non
  • volatile fraction contributes to pungency, colour, viscosity, flavour persistence and stability. Together
  • these fractions provide the complete sensory and functional properties of oleoresins.
  • Grading: Seeds are graded based on size, colour, cleanliness and quality.
  • Filtration: The extract is filtered to remove suspended solid particles.
  • Texture and mouthfeel
  • • Certain spices and spice ingredients influence the physical characteristics of food.
  • • Mustard seeds contribute texture to pickles, sauces and condiments.
  • • Sesame seeds add crunchiness to bakery products and confectionery.
  • • Spice powders can contribute body or thickness to some formulations, depending on the
  • product and quantity used.
  • Nutmeg
  • Active constituents: Myristicin, sabinene and pinene.
  • Dietary uses
  • • Used in cakes, pastries, puddings and confectionery.
  • • Added to dairy products, sauces, soups and meat preparations.
  • • Provides a warm, sweet and slightly nutty flavour.
  • Medicinal significance
  • • Traditionally used as a digestive aid.
  • • Contains compounds with antioxidant activity.
  • • Exhibits antimicrobial activity in laboratory studies.
  • Caution: Nutmeg should be used in normal culinary quantities because excessive consumption can
  • cause toxicity.

questions.question: Recall how antioxidant spices can contribute to food preservation. a). They help delay oxidative deterioration and maintain food quality b). They increase oxidation of fats c). They accelerate rancidity d). They reduce the storage stability of food
questions.solution_html:
• Culinary identity: Different combinations of spices produce the characteristic flavours of
  • regional and international cuisines.
  • Drying: Mace is dried under the sun or in a mechanical dryer at approximately 40–50°C until
  • the moisture content reaches about 8–10%.
  • Dietary fibre: Spent spice residues may contain fibre and other plant components that can be
  • evaluated for use in functional foods, bakery products and fibre supplements, subject to safety and
  • suitability.
  • Formation of supercritical CO₂ : Under these conditions, CO₂ exhibits properties of both liquids
  • and gases, enabling it to penetrate plant material and dissolve desirable compounds.
  • Proteins: Present in smaller quantities and contribute to its overall nutritional composition.
  • Aroma maturation: Conditioning or ageing allows flavour compounds to mature, producing a
  • richer, smoother and more complex aroma.
  • Reduced processing losses: Correct harvesting improves recovery of high-quality capsules
  • and reduces losses caused by immature or overripe produce.
  • Harvesting method
  • • Cardamom capsules do not mature uniformly on the plant.
  • • Therefore, harvesting is carried out manually at regular intervals, usually every 15–30 days
  • depending on the season and variety.
  • • Only mature capsules are collected, while immature capsules are left on the plant for further
  • development.
  • Harvesting at the correct stage ensures maximum yield, good essential oil content, attractive green
  • colour and superior commercial quality.
  • Cleaning and grading: Foreign matter is removed, and saffron is graded according to colour
  • aroma, purity and quality.
  • Roasting (optional): The seeds may be lightly roasted to enhance their characteristic aroma.
  • Solvent recovery: The solvent is removed, usually under controlled conditions, and recovered
  • for reuse where appropriate.
  • Improvement of overall acceptability
  • • Spices combine flavour, aroma, colour and mouthfeel to create a balanced sensory profile.
  • • They can make bland foods more appealing.
  • • Suitable spice combinations improve the identity and uniqueness of food products.
  • • Correct proportions are essential to avoid excessive pungency, bitterness or overpowering
  • aroma.
  • Mace
  • Active constituents: Myristicin and other volatile aromatic compounds.
  • Dietary uses
  • • Used in spice mixtures, bakery products and confectionery.
  • • Added to sauces, soups and meat preparations.
  • • Provides a warm, delicate and aromatic flavour.
  • Medicinal significance
  • • Traditionally used to support digestion.
  • • Contains aromatic compounds with antioxidant activity.
  • • Its volatile constituents have been investigated for potential biological activities.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: • Its volatile constituents have been investigated for potential biological activities.

questions.question: Examine the relationship between moisture content and spice trading. Which interpretation is most appropriate? a). Moisture can affect both product stability and the weight used for pricing b). Moisture has no effect on traded weight once the spice is graded c). Higher moisture always indicates better spice quality d). Moisture determination is mainly used to estimate volatile-oil composition
questions.solution_html:
• Grading and sorting: The dried mace is sorted according to colour, size, length of the blades
  • appearance and cleanliness. Damaged or inferior pieces are removed.
  • Natural pigments: Certain pigments may remain in the extraction residue, including curcuminoids
  • from turmeric and capsanthin from chilli, depending on the extraction method and conditions.
  • Extraction: Supercritical CO₂ is passed through the extraction vessel containing the prepared spice
  • material. It dissolves essential oils, oleoresins, natural pigments, pungent compounds and other
  • bioactive constituents.
  • Dietary fibre: Derived from the structural components of the dried fruit.
  • Improved market value: Properly cured beans have superior sensory quality, better appearance
  • and greater commercial value.
  • Four major stages of vanilla curing
  • • Killing: Stops normal physiological activities while preserving enzymes responsible for
  • flavour development.
  • • Sweating: Promotes enzymatic activity, vanillin formation, brown colour development and
  • aroma production.
  • • Drying: Gradually reduces moisture while maintaining flexibility and preventing spoilage.
  • • Conditioning (ageing): Allows flavour compounds to mature and stabilises the quality of
  • cured beans.
  • Packaging and storage: Saffron is packed in airtight, moisture-resistant containers and stored
  • in a cool, dark and dry place.
  • Essay Questions
  • Grinding: The seeds are ground into a fine or coarse powder, depending on the intended
  • application.
  • Oleoresin collection: The concentrated extract is collected.
  • Contribution to shelf life
  • • Some spices contain antioxidant and antimicrobial compounds that help delay oxidative
  • deterioration and microbial spoilage.
  • • Maintaining food quality during storage can help preserve its sensory acceptability.
  • Spices improve the sensory quality of food through their combined effects on flavour, taste, aroma
  • texture and colour. Proper selection and use of spices increase palatability and consumer acceptance.
  • Saffron
  • Active constituents: Crocin, picrocrocin and safranal.
  • Dietary uses
  • • Used in rice dishes, desserts, sweets and confectionery.
  • • Added to milk-based preparations and beverages.
  • • Crocin provides golden-yellow colour, picrocrocin contributes bitterness, and safranal
  • contributes characteristic aroma.
  • Medicinal significance
  • • Contains antioxidant compounds, particularly crocin.
  • • Has been studied for potential effects on mood and other aspects of health.
  • • Traditionally used in certain preparations to support general well-being.
  • Cinnamon, clove, fennel, fenugreek, nutmeg, mace and saffron have important dietary applications
  • because of their characteristic flavour, aroma and colour. Their bioactive constituents also contribute
  • to their traditional medicinal uses and are subjects of scientific research. However, these spices should
  • not replace prescribed medicines or established medical treatments.

questions.final_answer: not replace prescribed medicines or established medical treatments.

questions.question: Recognize the operation used to separate fenugreek seeds from harvested plants. a). Threshing b). Peeling c). Blanching d). Fermentation
questions.solution_html:
• Packaging: The dried mace is packed in airtight, moisture-proof packets or containers to
  • protect it from moisture and contamination.
  • Bioactive compounds: Residual polyphenols, flavonoids and other phytochemicals may remain in
  • the spent material and could be recovered for suitable applications.
  • Utilisation of by-products
  • • Spent spice residues and herbal biomass may be used for composting, organic fertiliser or
  • bioenergy production.
  • • Recovered solvents and CO₂ can be recycled to reduce costs and waste.
  • • Suitable residual fibre, pigments and bioactive compounds may be recovered for further
  • applications after quality and safety assessment.
  • Appropriate recovery and utilisation of oleoresin-processing by-products help minimise waste
  • improve resource efficiency and support sustainable spice processing.
  • Separation: The CO₂ carrying the dissolved compounds enters a separator. The pressure is
  • reduced, decreasing the solubility of the extracted compounds and allowing the oleoresin to separate
  • and be collected.
  • Minerals and moisture: Black pepper contains mineral constituents, while its moisture content
  • influences storage stability and quality.
  • Piperine is mainly responsible for pungency, while volatile oils contribute to the characteristic aroma.
  • The composition varies with variety, maturity, processing and storage conditions.
  • Sieving: The powder is sieved to obtain a uniform particle size.
  • Packaging and storage: The product is packed in suitable airtight containers and stored under
  • appropriate conditions.
  • Uses
  • • Used in processed foods, sauces, seasonings and spice blends.
  • • Provides consistent flavour in industrial food formulations.
  • • Used in food, pharmaceutical and cosmetic applications.
  • Coriander powder provides a convenient spice in powdered form, whereas coriander oleoresin
  • provides a concentrated flavouring ingredient suitable for standardised industrial applications.
